# How bacteria copy themselves and change

> *Bacteria change through errors in copying their own DNA and by acquiring DNA from other bacteria
> and from phages, and neither process aims at an outcome. Yet these undirected processes are enough
> to make bacteria resistant to drugs and to turn a harmless strain into a toxin producer.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Relate the differences between bacterial and human gene expression to the targets of drugs.
- Explain how random mutation and selection by a drug produce a resistant population.
- Distinguish transformation, transduction and conjugation, and explain how plasmids and
  transposons carry resistance and virulence genes.
- Contrast the lytic and lysogenic cycles of a phage, and explain lysogenic conversion.
- Describe the four mechanisms of antimicrobial resistance, and distinguish intrinsic from acquired
  resistance.
- Explain why antimicrobial stewardship depends on every prescriber.
:::

## Copying the genome {#sec-gen-copy}

A typical bacterium carries one circular chromosome. The chromosome of *Escherichia coli* has about
4.6 million base pairs and some 4,300 genes. Many bacteria also carry **plasmids**: small, circular
DNA molecules that replicate independently and often carry genes the cell can live without, such as
genes for resistance or toxins. Before dividing by binary fission, the cell copies its chromosome,
starting from a single origin and working round the circle in both directions.

Bacteria follow the same central dogma as human cells, with differences that matter clinically.

| Step | Human cells | Bacteria | Why the difference matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| Where it happens | Transcription in the nucleus, translation in the cytoplasm | Both in the cytoplasm at the same time: ribosomes start on an mRNA while it is still being made | Gene expression can change within minutes |
| Gene organisation | One gene per mRNA; genes interrupted by introns | Related genes often share one mRNA, as an **operon**; introns are rare | A whole pathway can be switched on at once |
| RNA polymerase | Several polymerases | One core enzyme of a different structure | A target human cells do not share |
| Ribosomes | 80S (40S and 60S subunits) | 70S (30S and 50S subunits) | A major drug target; mitochondria have bacterial-type ribosomes, which explains some drug side effects |
| DNA supercoiling | Human topoisomerases | DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV | A target with no exact human equivalent |

Each of these differences answers the question *what does it have that my cells lack?* for the
machinery of inheritance, and each is a possible basis for selective toxicity.

## How bacteria change {#sec-gen-change}

A bacterium gains a new trait in one of two ways: by a change in its own DNA, which passes to its
descendants (vertical inheritance), or by acquiring DNA from another bacterium, from a phage or from
its surroundings, which is **horizontal gene transfer**.

::: {.concept-tree}
[Routes of genetic change]{.tree-title}

- A new trait in a bacterium
  - Vertical: mutation in the cell's own DNA, inherited by its descendants
  - Horizontal: DNA acquired from another source
    - Transformation: free DNA taken up from dead cells
    - Transduction: bacterial DNA carried by a phage
    - Conjugation: a plasmid copied into a neighbour through direct contact
:::

### Mutation and selection {#sec-gen-mutation}

A **mutation** is a change in the DNA sequence. Most arise as copying errors during replication: a
**point mutation** replaces one base with another, while insertions and deletions add or remove bases.
DNA-based microbes make roughly one new mutation for every 300 genomes copied [@drake1991constant].
That rate sounds low, but bacterial populations are large, and resistance to a single drug can often
arise from any one of several different mutations. An infection containing billions of bacteria
usually already contains resistant mutants before treatment begins.

Most mutations are neutral or harmful. A few, by chance, alter the protein a drug acts on so that the
drug binds poorly. Whether the drug is present has no bearing on which mutations occur. Salvador Luria
and Max Delbrück showed this in 1943: the number of resistant bacteria varied widely between parallel
cultures, in the pattern expected if mutants arise at random during growth and not in response to the
selecting agent [@luria1943mutations]. Joshua and Esther Lederberg later showed it directly. Using
replica plating, they picked colonies from a plate that had never been exposed to the selecting agent
and found that they were already resistant [@lederberg1952replica].

Grow the population below, decide whether resistant cells exist yet, then add the drug.

<div data-island="selection-sim" data-src="/diagrams/selection-sim.yml"></div>

A drug kills the susceptible cells, and resistant cells that were already present multiply in their
place. This process is **selection**; repeated across many patients and many courses of
treatment, it makes resistance common.

::: {.callout-important}
## A common idea, corrected: "bacteria mutate in order to survive the drug"
In one study, 81% of undergraduates agreed that bacteria develop mutations *in order to* become
resistant [@richard2017intuitive]. Bacteria have no way of producing the mutation they need. Mutations
arise at random, and the drug selects the cells that happen to carry a useful one. Stress from some
drugs can raise the overall mutation rate a little, but the mutations remain random with respect to
resistance. A related belief, that the *body* becomes resistant, is held by 62.5% of Singapore
residents [@lim2021singaporekap]. Resistance is a property of bacteria, and resistant bacteria spread
between people.
:::

### Gene transfer {#sec-gen-hgt}

Three routes move genes between bacteria:

- **Transformation** is the uptake of free DNA released by dead cells. Some species are naturally
  **competent**: they actively take up DNA from their surroundings.
- **Transduction** occurs when a **bacteriophage**, a virus that infects bacteria, packages a piece of
  its host's DNA by mistake and injects it into the next bacterium it infects.
- **Conjugation** is the transfer of a plasmid from one cell to another through direct contact. A
  long **conjugative pilus**, distinct from the short attachment pili, draws the two cells together,
  and the DNA passes through a channel between them.

The older name "sex pilus" is misleading, because bacteria have no sexes and conjugation produces no
offspring. It copies a plasmid into a neighbouring cell, which can belong to a different species.

::: {.example}
Transformation was the first route discovered. In 1928 Frederick Griffith found that live,
unencapsulated *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, harmless on its own, killed mice when mixed with
heat-killed encapsulated cells ([Practise: Griffith's mice](#sec-gen-case)).
:::

**Transposons** ("jumping genes") move genes within and between DNA molecules. They are DNA segments
that can cut or copy themselves into a new position, for example from the chromosome onto a plasmid,
which can then carry them to another cell. Over time, plasmids and transposons collect several
resistance genes together, so a single transfer can confer resistance to several drugs.

Gene transfer also moves genes for **virulence**, the capacity to cause disease. Clusters of
virulence genes acquired together in this way are called **pathogenicity islands**.

::: {.example}
The *E. coli* strains that cause bloody diarrhoea carry an acquired pathogenicity island for
attaching to the gut lining, which the harmless gut strains lack.
:::

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-vertical-horizontal.yml"></div>

### Bacteriophages: lytic and lysogenic cycles {#sec-gen-phage}

Phages are the most numerous biological entities on Earth. After injecting its genome, a phage
follows one of two paths. In the **lytic cycle**, the phage multiplies and **lyses** (bursts) the
cell. In the **lysogenic cycle**, the phage genome joins the bacterial chromosome as a **prophage**.

|  | Lytic cycle | Lysogenic cycle |
|---|---|---|
| What the phage genome does | Takes over the cell and directs it to make hundreds of new phages | Joins the chromosome and is copied with it each time the cell divides |
| Fate of the bacterium | Lysed, releasing the new phages | Survives and multiplies |
| Effect on the bacterium's traits | None that last, because the cell dies | Prophage genes can give the bacterium new traits |

Damage to the bacterium's DNA can later switch a prophage into the lytic cycle.

A prophage can change what its host does, which is called **lysogenic conversion**. Several of the
best-known bacterial toxins are encoded by prophage genes, so only the strains that carry the prophage
are **toxigenic** (toxin-producing).

::: {.example}
The Shiga toxins made by *E. coli* strains that cause bloody diarrhoea are encoded by prophage genes;
gut *E. coli* without the prophage makes no toxin.
:::

The same species can therefore be harmless or dangerous depending on which phages it carries.

## Antimicrobial resistance {#sec-gen-resistance}

### Mechanisms of resistance {#sec-gen-mechanisms}

**Antimicrobial resistance** is the ability of a microbe to grow in the presence of a drug that would
normally inhibit or kill it. Some resistance is **intrinsic**, a property of the whole species.

::: {.example}
*Mycoplasma* has no cell wall, so drugs that act on the wall cannot affect it.
:::

Most clinically important resistance is **acquired**, by mutation or gene transfer. Whatever its
origin, resistance works in one of four ways.

| Mechanism | How it works | Usual genetic origin |
|---|---|---|
| Destroy or modify the drug | An enzyme breaks the drug down, or adds a chemical group that stops it binding its target | Genes on plasmids and transposons |
| Change the target | The drug's target protein is altered so the drug binds poorly | Mutation, or an acquired gene for a different version of the target |
| Keep the drug out | Fewer **porins**, the channels in the Gram-negative outer membrane, let less drug in | Mutation |
| Pump the drug out | **Efflux pumps** in the membrane expel the drug | Mutation increasing pump production, or acquired pump genes |

::: {.example}
Meticillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus* (MRSA) has acquired a gene for an altered version of the
protein that meticillin and related drugs act on, so the drugs bind it poorly [@lakhundi2018mrsa]
([*Gram-positive cocci*](../microbes/gram-positive-cocci.qmd#sec-gpc-supporting)).
:::

### Selection and stewardship {#sec-gen-stewardship}

Every use of an antimicrobial, in people or in animals, selects resistant bacteria. Resistance genes
on plasmids pass between species, so a drug used against one organism can enrich genes that later
reach another. Resistance often carries a cost: without the drug, resistant bacteria may grow a little
more slowly, which is one reason resistance can decline when drug use falls, although many resistance
genes persist for years.

**Antimicrobial stewardship** is the coordinated effort to use antimicrobials only when they are
needed, at the right dose and for the right duration, so that selection is kept to a minimum. Because
resistance is selected by the total use of antimicrobials in a population, stewardship depends on
every prescriber.
